```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "")
# Console colour carries no meaning on a rendered page. pkgdown turns it on for
# its own build, and the escape sequences then reach the reader as literal text,
# so colour is switched off here for a plain vignette render and a site build
# alike. The fixed width keeps tibbles inside the documentation column.
options(cli.num_colors = 1, cli.hyperlink = FALSE, crayon.enabled = FALSE,
        width = 80)
# Print data frames and tibbles as formatted tables.
local({
  kp <- function(x, ...) {
    if (any(vapply(x, is.list, logical(1)))) return(knitr::normal_print(x))
    knitr::knit_print(knitr::kable(x))
  }
  for (cls in c("data.frame", "tbl_df", "tbl")) {
    registerS3method("knit_print", cls, kp, envir = asNamespace("knitr"))
  }
})
```

```{r setup}
library(scopusflow)
```

`scopus_query()` composes field-tagged 'Scopus' queries from separate terms. A
query pasted together by hand can contain a missing bracket or a mistyped tag
and return the wrong records without an error. Composing a query is string
construction and runs offline without an API key. Each call is shown with the
literal query string it returns. The steps that size or run a search contact
the API, so they are shown but not run.

## Field tags decide where to look

A field tag restricts a query to part of a record. `scopus_field_tags()` lists
the common ones.

```{r}
scopus_field_tags()
```

The most generally useful tag is `TITLE-ABS-KEY`, which searches the title,
abstract and keywords together. It is broad enough to find work on a topic
without the incidental matches of a full-text search.

## One term, many disciplines

`scopus_query()` works the same way in any discipline. Each call below returns
the exact query string that would be sent to 'Scopus'.

```{r}
# molecular biology
scopus_query("CRISPR", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")
scopus_query("gravitational waves", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY") # physics
# environmental science
scopus_query("microplastics", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")
scopus_query("blockchain", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")          # computer science
scopus_query("digital humanities", .field = "AUTHKEY")        # humanities
```

The last example uses `AUTHKEY`, the author-supplied keywords. It finds work
whose authors chose the term as a keyword and so returns fewer records that
mention it only in passing.

## Combining terms with boolean operators

Passing several terms joins them into one query. The default operator is `AND`,
and `OR` or `AND NOT` are available through the `.op` argument.

```{r}
# Two concepts that must co-occur (materials science).
scopus_query("perovskite", "solar cell", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")

# Two names for one condition, either of which will do (medicine). writeLines()
# shows the quotation marks without the backslashes R prints to escape them.
writeLines(scopus_query('"heart attack"', '"myocardial infarction"', .op = "OR"))

# A family of related tools (molecular biology).
scopus_query("CRISPR", "Cas9", "Cas12", .op = "OR")

# Excluding a dominant homonym, so the snake stays out of the results.
scopus_query("python", "snake", .op = "AND NOT", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")
```

## Phrases

'Scopus' joins the words of an unquoted term with AND, so `heart attack` finds
records that mention both words anywhere in the searched field. Double
quotation marks ask for a loose phrase, whose words must be adjacent, although
punctuation is ignored and plurals are included. Braces ask for an exact phrase,
including any stop words, spaces and punctuation. Elsevier's
[search tips](https://dev.elsevier.com/sc_search_tips.html) describe all three.

```{r}
writeLines(scopus_query('"heart attack"', .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")) # loose phrase
writeLines(scopus_query("{heart attack}", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")) # exact phrase
```

`scopus_query()` leaves both kinds of phrase as written. When terms are joined
without a field tag, a term of several unquoted words is put in brackets, so it
stays one operand of the join. Without the brackets, the first query below
would read as `machine AND (learning OR deep) AND learning`.

```{r}
writeLines(scopus_query("machine learning", "deep learning", .op = "OR"))
writeLines(scopus_query('"machine learning"', '"deep learning"', .op = "OR"))
```

## Brackets in a query written by hand

A query that mixes operators needs brackets to make its grouping unambiguous.
The search tips state that 'Scopus' applies OR first, then AND, then AND NOT, so
`A AND NOT B AND C` reads as `A AND NOT (B AND C)`. Elsevier has announced a new
order, with AND NOT first, then AND, then OR
([Feldner, 2025](https://blog.scopus.com/boolean-searches-in-scopus-understanding-operator-precedence-best-practices/)),
under which `A OR B AND C` reads as `A OR (B AND C)`. Brackets give the same
reading under either order.

The package brackets the strings it composes. `scopus_compare_topics()` and
`scopus_intersections()` bracket each side of their joins. The year limit of a
plan, a count or a trend is sent as a separate request parameter and is never
added to the query string. A query built by an earlier `scopus_query()` call
stays one operand when it is joined again, as in the example below.

```{r}
young <- scopus_query("children", "adolescents", .op = "OR")
scopus_query("vaccine", young)
```

## From a query to a plan

A composed query can be passed directly to the rest of the workflow. The example
below uses it as the query of a year-partitioned plan, which keeps each cell
under the API's 5000-record ceiling for offset paging, provided that no single
year matches more than 5000 records.

```{r}
q <- scopus_query("gut microbiome", "immunology", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")
q
plan <- scopus_plan(q, years = 2015:2022, partition = "year")
plan
```

Sizing and running the plan contact the API, so the two calls below are not run
here.

```{r eval = FALSE}
scopus_count(q, years = 2015:2022)
records <- scopus_fetch_plan(plan)
```

Without a key, `vignette("scopusflow")` follows the same two steps through to a
record set. 'Scopus' records may not be redistributed, so the bundled corpus of
published articles stands in for the harvest.

## Searching by affiliation

Field tags can also search parts of a record that do not describe its topic.
`AFFILORG` searches the affiliation organisation name, so a query can retrieve
the output of an institution.

```{r}
scopus_query("Max Planck", .field = "AFFILORG")
```

## When a term is empty

`scopus_query()` checks its terms as it builds the query. An empty or
whitespace-only term raises `scopus_error_bad_input` before a malformed query
can be produced.

```{r}
tryCatch(
  scopus_query("graphene", ""),
  scopus_error_bad_input = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

## Checks before any request

`scopus_plan()`, `scopus_count()`, `scopus_fetch()`, `scopus_trend()`,
`scopus_compare_topics()` and `scopus_intersections()` check each query offline
before anything is sent and raise `scopus_error_bad_input` for three mistakes.
Refinement syntax copied from the web interface, such as
`LIMIT-TO(DOCTYPE, "ar")`, is ignored by the Search API, so the search would run
unfiltered with no sign of a problem. A field tag wrapped around a query that
already opens with one is rejected by the API. A bracket, quotation mark or
brace left unclosed changes what the rest of the query means. The message of
each error says what to write instead.

```{r}
tryCatch(
  scopus_plan('working memory AND (LIMIT-TO (DOCTYPE, "ar"))'),
  scopus_error_bad_input = function(e) writeLines(strwrap(conditionMessage(e), 76))
)
```

Written as search fields, the same limits pass the check.

```{r}
scopus_plan("working memory AND DOCTYPE(ar) AND LANGUAGE(english)")$query
```

A strategy pasted from the advanced search with its own tags, such as
`TITLE-ABS-KEY ( "working memory" )`, is sent as written when `field` is left
as `NULL`. `INDEXTERMS()`, which pybliometrics documents as not working through
the Search API, raises a warning. `KEY()` searches the index terms together with
author keywords, trade names and chemical names.

## Checking recall against known records

A search strategy can be tested against records that are already known to be
relevant and were collected independently of it, for instance the studies
included in an earlier review or those named by experts. The share of them the
strategy retrieves is its relative recall
([Sampson et al., 2006](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-6-33)), and
[Bramer et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2018.283) make the check a
step in developing a search.

The check runs two searches for each chain of DOIs joined by OR, both under the
same year limit. The chain alone finds which known records 'Scopus' indexes, and
the strategy joined to the chain finds which of those it retrieves. A known
record the chain does not find, because 'Scopus' does not index it or holds it
without that DOI, cannot show whether the strategy finds it. It is left out of
the denominator and listed, so it can be checked by hand.

The sketch below contacts the API, so it is not run here. Its DOIs are
placeholders for your own. `scopus_extract_dois()` strips resolver prefixes from
them and removes duplicates without regard to case, and the sketch compares DOIs
in lower case, so a resolver prefix or a difference in case does no harm. Chains
of at most 25 DOIs keep each request short. How the API treats much longer
chains has not been checked.

```{r eval = FALSE}
known <- scopus_extract_dois(
  c("10.xxxx/known-1", "https://doi.org/10.xxxx/known-2", "doi:10.xxxx/known-3")
)
strategy <- scopus_query("working memory", "training", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")
years <- 2010:2024

chains <- vapply(
  split(known, ceiling(seq_along(known) / 25)),
  function(dois) paste(sprintf('DOI("%s")', dois), collapse = " OR "),
  character(1)
)
found <- function(query) {
  tolower(scopus_extract_dois(scopus_fetch(query, years = years)))
}

indexed <- unique(unlist(lapply(chains, found)))
retrieved <- unique(unlist(lapply(chains, function(chain) {
  found(sprintf("(%s) AND (%s)", strategy, chain))
})))
not_found <- setdiff(tolower(known), indexed)
relative_recall <- length(retrieved) / length(indexed)
```

The relative recall describes the strategy against this reference set alone, so
report the set, its source and the DOIs left out alongside it.
